notes.front: What is the ozone layer, and where is it?
notes.back: The layer in the stratosphere, about 15 to 30 km (9 to 18 miles) above the surface, where most atmospheric ozone is concentrated.
notes.explanation: Ozone is a molecule of three oxygen atoms. In the stratosphere its molecules are constantly being formed and destroyed at the same time.
notes.example: Like a sunscreen spread through the sky 15 to 30 km up, well above the lowest layer where almost all weather happens.
notes.evidence: Most atmospheric ozone is concentrated in a layer in the stratosphere, about 9 to 18 miles (15 to 30 km) above the Earth's surface (see the figure). Ozone is a molecule that contains three oxygen atoms. At any given time, ozone molecules are constantly formed and destroyed in the stratosphere.
notes.source: US EPA, Basic Ozone Layer Science, “I. The Ozone Layer”

notes.front: What is ultraviolet B (UVB), and how much of it does ozone absorb?
notes.back: One of the three bands of the sun's ultraviolet light. Ozone absorbs most of it, although some reaches the Earth.
notes.explanation: Of the three bands, ozone does not absorb ultraviolet A at all and absorbs ultraviolet C completely; UVB sits between, mostly but not fully absorbed.
notes.example: Like a blind that is mostly shut: most UVB is stopped high up, but some still reaches your skin on a sunny day.
notes.evidence: The sun produces UV, which is commonly split into three bands: UVA, UVB, and UVC. UVA is not absorbed by ozone. UVB is mostly absorbed by ozone, although some reaches the Earth. UVC is completely absorbed by ozone and normal oxygen.
notes.source: US EPA, Basic Ozone Layer Science, introduction (glossary entry “ultraviolet (UV) light”)

notes.front: What is an ozone-depleting substance (ODS)?
notes.back: A compound that releases chlorine or bromine when exposed to intense ultraviolet light in the stratosphere, and so contributes to ozone depletion.
notes.explanation: The label turns on what the compound does high up: freeing chlorine or bromine in the stratosphere is what makes it contribute to depletion.
notes.example: Like a parcel that travels unopened: it rises intact from ground level and only lets go of its chlorine or bromine once ultraviolet light breaks it apart.
notes.evidence: Some compounds release chlorine or bromine when they are exposed to intense UV light in the stratosphere. These compounds contribute to ozone depletion, and are called ozone-depleting substances
notes.source: US EPA, Basic Ozone Layer Science, “II. Ozone Depletion”

notes.front: What is a chlorofluorocarbon (CFC)?
notes.back: A compound of chlorine, fluorine and carbon, commonly used as a refrigerant, a solvent or a foam blowing agent.
notes.explanation: CFCs are very stable in the lower atmosphere, move up to the stratosphere, and are broken down there by strong ultraviolet light, releasing chlorine atoms that deplete the ozone layer.
notes.example: Like CFC-114 or CFC-115: two of the five most common CFCs, with no hydrogen in the molecule.
notes.evidence: A compound consisting of chlorine, fluorine, and carbon. CFCs are very stable in the troposphere. They move to the stratosphere and are broken down by strong ultraviolet (UV) light, where they release chlorine atoms that then deplete the ozone layer. CFCs are commonly used as refrigerants, solvents, and foam blowing agents.
notes.source: US EPA, Section 608 Technician Certification Test Topics, Core, “Environmental Impacts” (glossary entry “chlorofluorocarbon”)

notes.front: What is a hydrochlorofluorocarbon (HCFC)?
notes.back: A compound of hydrogen, chlorine, fluorine and carbon: one class of chemicals used to replace CFCs.
notes.explanation: HCFCs still contain chlorine, and so still deplete stratospheric ozone, but to a much lesser extent than CFCs.
notes.example: Like HCFC-123, used in centrifugal chillers: a CFC-style molecule with hydrogen added.
notes.evidence: A compound consisting of hydrogen, chlorine, fluorine, and carbon. The HCFCs are one class of chemicals being used to replace the CFCs. They contain chlorine and thus deplete stratospheric ozone, but to a much lesser extent than CFCs.
notes.source: US EPA, Section 608 Technician Certification Test Topics, Core, “Environmental Impacts” (glossary entry “hydrochlorofluorocarbon”)

notes.front: What is a hydrofluorocarbon (HFC)?
notes.back: A compound of hydrogen, fluorine and carbon: a class of replacements for CFCs.
notes.explanation: With no chlorine or bromine in the molecule, HFCs do not deplete the ozone layer.
notes.example: Like an HCFC with the chlorine taken out: only hydrogen, fluorine and carbon are left.
notes.evidence: A compound consisting of hydrogen, fluorine, and carbon. The HFCs are a class of replacements for CFCs. Because they do not contain chlorine or bromine, they do not deplete the ozone layer.
notes.source: US EPA, Section 608 Technician Certification Test Topics, Core, “Environmental Impacts” (glossary entry “hydrofluorocarbon”)

notes.front: What is ozone depletion potential (ODP)?
notes.back: A number for the ozone depletion a substance causes, compared with a similar mass of CFC-11, whose ODP is defined as 1.0.
notes.explanation: CFC-11 is the yardstick, so a substance with an ODP of 0.5 does half the ozone damage of the same mass of CFC-11.
notes.example: Like pricing everything in one currency: CFC-11 is fixed at 1.0, and every other substance is quoted against it.
notes.evidence: A number that refers to the amount of ozone depletion caused by a substance. The ODP is the ratio of the impact on ozone of a chemical compared to the impact of a similar mass of CFC-11. Thus, the ODP of CFC-11 is defined to be 1.0.
notes.source: US EPA, Section 608 Technician Certification Test Topics, Core, “Environmental Impacts” (glossary entry “ozone depletion potential”)

notes.front: Under the federal refrigerant regulations, what is a class I substance?
notes.back: An ozone-depleting substance listed in appendix A to subpart A of part 82 of Title 40.
notes.explanation: The definition works by list: a substance is class I because it appears in that appendix, not because of a property named in the definition itself.
notes.example: Like a named list of controlled goods: CFC-11 is on the class I list, so the class I rules follow it wherever it is used.
notes.evidence: Class I refers to an ozone-depleting substance that is listed in 40 CFR part 82 subpart A, appendix A.
notes.source: 40 CFR 82.152 (eCFR), definition of “Class I”

notes.front: What is a class II substance?
notes.back: An ozone-depleting substance with an ODP of less than 0.2. Every class II substance is an HCFC.
notes.explanation: So the whole class is made up of hydrochlorofluorocarbons, each under the 0.2 line of ozone depletion potential.
notes.example: Like HCFC-141b, once used as a solvent and foam-blowing agent: an HCFC, and so a class II substance.
notes.evidence: less than 0.2, and are all hydrochlorofluorocarbons
notes.source: US EPA, Phaseout of Class II Ozone-Depleting Substances, introduction

notes.front: In the federal refrigerant regulations, what is a substitute?
notes.back: Any chemical or product, existing or new, used as a refrigerant to replace a class I or class II ozone-depleting substance.
notes.explanation: A substitute is defined by the job it does, replacing a class I or II refrigerant, whether the chemical is old or new; the listed examples are open-ended.
notes.example: Like a new cast member taking an old role: carbon dioxide charged into a new system in place of an HCFC is a substitute.
notes.evidence: Substitute means any chemical or product, whether existing or new, that is used as a refrigerant to replace a class I or II ozone-depleting substance. Examples include, but are not limited to hydrofluorocarbons, perfluorocarbons, hydrofluoroolefins, hydrofluoroethers, hydrocarbons, ammonia, carbon dioxide, and blends thereof.
notes.source: 40 CFR 82.152 (eCFR), definition of “Substitute”

notes.front: What happens when chlorine or bromine atoms come into contact with ozone in the stratosphere?
notes.back: They destroy ozone molecules.
notes.explanation: The destruction can then run faster than ozone is naturally created, and a single chlorine atom destroys a great many molecules before it is removed.
notes.evidence: When chlorine and bromine atoms come into contact with ozone in the stratosphere, they destroy ozone molecules. One chlorine atom can destroy over 100,000 ozone molecules before it is removed from the stratosphere. Ozone can be destroyed more quickly than it is naturally created.
notes.source: US EPA, Basic Ozone Layer Science, “II. Ozone Depletion”

notes.front: One chlorine atom can destroy over {{c1::100,000}} ozone molecules before it is removed from the stratosphere.
notes.explanation: The figure is per atom: each chlorine atom goes on destroying ozone until it is finally removed from the stratosphere.
notes.evidence: One chlorine atom can destroy over 100,000 ozone molecules before it is removed from the stratosphere.
notes.source: US EPA, Basic Ozone Layer Science, “II. Ozone Depletion”

notes.front: Why are there no natural processes that remove ODS from the lower atmosphere?
notes.back: ODS are very stable and do not dissolve in rain.
notes.explanation: The source draws a contrast with chlorine from swimming pools, industrial plants, sea salt and volcanoes, which does not reach the stratosphere at all.
notes.evidence: chlorine from swimming pools, industrial plants, sea salt, and volcanoes does not reach the stratosphere. In contrast, ODS are very stable and do not dissolve in rain. Thus, there are no natural processes that remove the ODS from the lower atmosphere.
notes.source: US EPA, Basic Ozone Layer Science, “II. Ozone Depletion”

notes.front: ODS emitted at the Earth's surface are eventually carried into the stratosphere, in a process that can take as long as {{c1::two to five years}}.
notes.explanation: The source says “can take as long as”, so this is an upper range, not a fixed delay: a release today may reach the ozone layer years later.
notes.evidence: they are eventually carried into the stratosphere in a process that can take as long as two to five years
notes.source: US EPA, Basic Ozone Layer Science, “II. Ozone Depletion”

notes.front: A trainee says chlorine from swimming pools and sea salt must be a major cause of ozone depletion, since chlorine destroys ozone. Is the trainee right?
notes.back: No. Chlorine from swimming pools, industrial plants, sea salt and volcanoes does not reach the stratosphere.
notes.explanation: What matters is whether the chlorine gets to the stratosphere. ODS do, because they are very stable and are not washed out by rain.
notes.evidence: chlorine from swimming pools, industrial plants, sea salt, and volcanoes does not reach the stratosphere. In contrast, ODS are very stable and do not dissolve in rain. Thus, there are no natural processes that remove the ODS from the lower atmosphere.
notes.source: US EPA, Basic Ozone Layer Science, “II. Ozone Depletion”

notes.front: Which ODS, generally used as fire extinguishing agents, contain bromine?
notes.back: Halons (also called bromofluorocarbons).
notes.explanation: Bromine is many times more effective at destroying stratospheric ozone than chlorine.
notes.evidence: Compounds, also known as bromofluorocarbons, that contain bromine, fluorine, and carbon. They are generally used as fire extinguishing agents and cause ozone depletion. Bromine is many times more effective at destroying stratospheric ozone than chlorine.
notes.source: US EPA, Basic Ozone Layer Science, “II. Ozone Depletion” (glossary entry “halons”)

notes.front: Do HCFCs deplete stratospheric ozone, and how do they compare with CFCs?
notes.back: Yes, because they contain chlorine, but to a much lesser extent than CFCs.
notes.explanation: HCFCs are one class of chemicals being used to replace CFCs; the chlorine they still carry is what makes them ozone-depleting.
notes.evidence: The HCFCs are one class of chemicals being used to replace the CFCs. They contain chlorine and thus deplete stratospheric ozone, but to a much lesser extent than CFCs.
notes.source: US EPA, Section 608 Technician Certification Test Topics, Core, “Environmental Impacts” (glossary entry “hydrochlorofluorocarbon”)

notes.front: HCFCs have ozone depletion potentials ranging from {{c1::0.01 to 0.1}}.
notes.explanation: Set against CFC-11, fixed at 1.0 by definition, even the top of this range is a tenth of the reference.
notes.evidence: HCFCs have ozone depletion potentials (ODPs) ranging from 0.01 to 0.1.
notes.source: US EPA, Section 608 Technician Certification Test Topics, Core, “Environmental Impacts” (glossary entry “hydrochlorofluorocarbon”)

notes.front: What ODP do CFC-11 and CFC-12 each have?
notes.back: 1 each.
notes.explanation: They are two of the five most common CFCs; the other three are CFC-113 (0.8), CFC-114 (1) and CFC-115 (0.6).
notes.evidence: The most common CFCs are CFC-11, CFC-12, CFC-113, CFC-114, and CFC-115. The ozone depletion potential (ODP) for each CFC is, respectively, 1, 1, 0.8, 1, and 0.6.
notes.source: US EPA, Section 608 Technician Certification Test Topics, Core, “Environmental Impacts” (glossary entry “chlorofluorocarbon”)

notes.front: How do CFCs, HCFCs and HFCs rank by ozone depletion potential, highest first?
notes.back: CFCs, then HCFCs, then HFCs.
notes.explanation: The test outline lists this ranking among the core environmental ideas a technician is tested on.
notes.evidence: than HCFCs, which in turn have higher ODP than HFCs
notes.source: US EPA, Section 608 Technician Certification Test Topics, Core, “Environmental Impacts”

notes.front: HFCs have an ODP of {{c1::zero}}, because they do not contain chlorine.
notes.explanation: Chlorine is what an ODS frees in the stratosphere to destroy ozone, and an HFC molecule has none to free.
notes.evidence: HFCs have zero ODP because they do not contain chlorine.
notes.source: US EPA, Section 608 Technician Certification Test Topics, Core, “Environmental Impacts” (glossary entry “ozone depletion potential”)

notes.front: Which group of ODS has ozone depletion potentials ranging up to 10?
notes.back: The halons.
notes.explanation: Two other ODS sit either side of CFC-11: carbon tetrachloride at 1.2 and methyl chloroform at 0.11.
notes.evidence: The halons have ODPs ranging up to 10. Carbon tetrachloride has an ODP of 1.2, and methyl chloroform's ODP is 0.11.
notes.source: US EPA, Section 608 Technician Certification Test Topics, Core, “Environmental Impacts” (glossary entry “ozone depletion potential”)

notes.front: HFCs are not ozone-depleting substances. What environmental harm do they still do?
notes.back: They are potent greenhouse gases that contribute to climate change.
notes.explanation: The same answer notes that, from 1 January 2018, buying HFCs for stationary refrigeration and air-conditioning systems requires technician certification.
notes.evidence: Beginning January 1, 2018 EPA technician certification (EPA Section 608 certification) is required to purchase HFCs for use in stationary refrigeration and air-conditioning systems. While HFCs are not ozone-depleting substances, they are potent greenhouse gases that contribute to climate change.
notes.source: US EPA, Technicians and Contractors: Frequent Questions, “Are there any restrictions on the purchase of hydrofluorocarbon (HFC) refrigerants?”

notes.front: What ozone depletion potential marks a class I ODS?
notes.back: An ODP of 0.2 or higher.
notes.explanation: The class I groups include the halons, the ODS with the highest ODPs of all.
notes.evidence: of 0.2 or higher, and include halons,
notes.source: US EPA, Phaseout of Class I Ozone-Depleting Substances, introduction

notes.front: What were HCFCs originally developed as?
notes.back: Transitional substitutes for class I ODS.
notes.explanation: They were a stop-gap: HCFCs still contain chlorine and deplete ozone, so they too are being phased out, on a later schedule than class I substances.
notes.evidence: HCFCs were developed as transitional substitutes for Class I ODS and are subject to a later phaseout schedule than Class I ODS.
notes.source: US EPA, Phaseout of Class II Ozone-Depleting Substances, introduction

notes.front: A system runs on R-401A, a blend containing HCFC-22 that is not itself one of the 34 listed HCFCs. Do the class II rules apply to it?
notes.back: Yes. Blends that contain a class II ODS are subject to the same rules.
notes.explanation: Containing HCFC-22 is enough: R-401A is one of the common blends the source names as falling under the same rules.
notes.evidence: While these blends are not listed among the 34 controlled HCFCs, they are subject to the same rules because they contain Class II ODS. Common refrigerant blends that contain HCFC-22 included R-401A, R-402A, R-408A, R-409A, R-414B, and R-502A.
notes.source: US EPA, Phaseout of Class II Ozone-Depleting Substances, introduction

notes.front: Is CFC-12 a class I or a class II ozone-depleting substance?
notes.back: Class I.
notes.explanation: The Clean Air Act splits ODS into two groups, and chlorofluorocarbons are the example given for class I.
notes.evidence: The ODS are split into two groups under the Clean Air Act: Class I ODS, such as chlorofluorocarbons
notes.source: US EPA, Ozone-Depleting Substances, introduction

notes.front: Is HCFC-123, used in centrifugal chillers, a class I or a class II substance?
notes.back: Class II.
notes.explanation: Class II substances are all HCFCs, so any HCFC is class II whatever it is used for.
notes.evidence: less than 0.2, and are all hydrochlorofluorocarbons
notes.source: US EPA, Phaseout of Class II Ozone-Depleting Substances, introduction

notes.front: Which kind of refrigerant is R-12: CFC, HCFC or HFC?
notes.back: A CFC.
notes.explanation: The test expects you to place a refrigerant by its number, not its chemical formula: R-12 is the outline's own example of a CFC.
notes.evidence: not chemical formulas, but idea that R-12 is a CFC, R-22 is an HCFC, R-134 is an HFC
notes.source: US EPA, Section 608 Technician Certification Test Topics, Core, “Environmental Impacts”

notes.front: Which kind of refrigerant is R-22: CFC, HCFC or HFC?
notes.back: An HCFC.
notes.explanation: The outline pairs R-22 with the HCFC class; the number, not the formula, is what you are expected to recognise.
notes.evidence: not chemical formulas, but idea that R-12 is a CFC, R-22 is an HCFC, R-134 is an HFC
notes.source: US EPA, Section 608 Technician Certification Test Topics, Core, “Environmental Impacts”

notes.front: Which kind of refrigerant is R-134a: CFC, HCFC or HFC?
notes.back: An HFC: R-134a is another name for HFC-134a.
notes.explanation: The outline names HFC-134a, also called R-134a, as a likely substitute for a CFC refrigerant.
notes.evidence: (HFC)-134a (also called R-134a) as likely substitute for
notes.source: US EPA, Section 608 Technician Certification Test Topics, Type 1 (Small Appliances)

notes.front: Three cylinders sit on a van: R-12, R-22 and R-134a. Which refrigerant has the lowest ozone depletion potential?
notes.back: B: R-134a, an HFC.
notes.choicesExplained: A is wrong: R-12 is a CFC, the highest of the three classes. B is wrong: R-22 is an HCFC, below a CFC but still above an HFC.
notes.explanation: The ranking runs CFCs, then HCFCs, then HFCs, so the HFC is lowest.
notes.evidence: than HCFCs, which in turn have higher ODP than HFCs
notes.source: US EPA, Section 608 Technician Certification Test Topics, Core, “Environmental Impacts”

notes.front: A colleague shrugs off a small release of CFC refrigerant: “It's only a few grams.” Which fact about chlorine answers this?
notes.back: One chlorine atom can destroy over 100,000 ozone molecules before it is removed from the stratosphere.
notes.explanation: Each chlorine atom released in the stratosphere keeps destroying ozone, so a few grams carry a great many destructive atoms.
notes.evidence: One chlorine atom can destroy over 100,000 ozone molecules before it is removed from the stratosphere.
notes.source: US EPA, Basic Ozone Layer Science, “II. Ozone Depletion”

notes.front: A customer insists on an HFC refrigerant because “HFCs are harmless to the environment”. What is the accurate reply?
notes.back: HFCs are not ozone-depleting substances, but they are potent greenhouse gases that contribute to climate change.
notes.explanation: Zero ozone depletion is not zero harm: the climate effect is the concern with HFCs.
notes.evidence: While HFCs are not ozone-depleting substances, they are potent greenhouse gases that contribute to climate change.
notes.source: US EPA, Technicians and Contractors: Frequent Questions, “Are there any restrictions on the purchase of hydrofluorocarbon (HFC) refrigerants?”

notes.front: An industrial system is designed to run on ammonia instead of an HCFC. Is the ammonia a substitute under the regulations?
notes.back: Yes. Ammonia is one of the listed examples of substitutes.
notes.explanation: A substitute is any chemical used as a refrigerant to replace a class I or II ODS, and the definition's open list names ammonia.
notes.evidence: Examples include, but are not limited to hydrofluorocarbons, perfluorocarbons, hydrofluoroolefins, hydrofluoroethers, hydrocarbons, ammonia, carbon dioxide, and blends thereof.
notes.source: 40 CFR 82.152 (eCFR), definition of “Substitute”

notes.front: What do laboratory and epidemiological studies show about UVB and skin cancer?
notes.back: UVB causes non-melanoma skin cancer and plays a major role in the development of malignant melanoma.
notes.explanation: Of the human health effects from sun exposure, melanoma is the most lethal.
notes.evidence: Laboratory and epidemiological studies demonstrate that UVB causes non-melanoma skin cancer and plays a major role in malignant melanoma development. Of the human health effects from sun exposure, melanoma is the most lethal
notes.source: US EPA, Health and Environmental Effects of Ozone Layer Depletion, “Effects on Human Health”

notes.front: Which eye condition, a clouding of the lens, has been linked to UVB?
notes.back: Cataracts.
notes.explanation: The source lists it in addition to skin cancer among the human health effects of UVB.
notes.evidence: In addition, UVB has been linked to the development of cataracts, a clouding of the eye's lens.
notes.source: US EPA, Health and Environmental Effects of Ozone Layer Depletion, “Effects on Human Health”

notes.front: How does solar UVB affect phytoplankton?
notes.back: It affects their orientation and motility, reducing survival, and ozone depletion-related UVB increases directly reduce their production.
notes.explanation: Scientists have measured the drop in phytoplankton production, so this is a demonstrated effect, not only a forecast.
notes.evidence: Exposure to solar UVB radiation has been shown to affect both orientation and motility in phytoplankton, resulting in reduced survival rates for these organisms. Scientists have demonstrated a direct reduction in phytoplankton production due to ozone depletion-related increases in UVB.
notes.source: US EPA, Health and Environmental Effects of Ozone Layer Depletion, “Effects on Marine Ecosystems”

notes.front: What are the most severe effects of UVB on fish, shrimp, crab and other marine animals?
notes.back: Decreased reproductive capacity and impaired larval development.
notes.explanation: The damage falls on the early developmental stages of these animals.
notes.evidence: UVB radiation has been found to cause damage to early developmental stages of fish, shrimp, crab, amphibians, and other marine animals. The most severe effects are decreased reproductive capacity and impaired larval development.
notes.source: US EPA, Health and Environmental Effects of Ozone Layer Depletion, “Effects on Marine Ecosystems”

notes.front: Besides direct damage, how can UVB affect plants?
notes.back: Through indirect changes, such as in plant form or the timing of developmental phases.
notes.explanation: The source hedges: these indirect changes may be equally or sometimes more important than the damaging effects, not always.
notes.evidence: Indirect changes caused by UVB (such as changes in plant form, how nutrients are distributed within the plant, timing of developmental phases and secondary metabolism) may be equally or sometimes more important than damaging effects of UVB.
notes.source: US EPA, Health and Environmental Effects of Ozone Layer Depletion, “Effects on Plants”

notes.front: What will increased UVB do to synthetic polymers used outdoors?
notes.back: Accelerate their breakdown, shortening the time they stay useful outdoors.
notes.explanation: Special additives give today's materials some protection from UVB, but only some.
notes.evidence: Today's materials are somewhat protected from UVB by special additives. Yet, increases in UVB levels will accelerate their breakdown, limiting the length of time for which they are useful outdoors.
notes.source: US EPA, Health and Environmental Effects of Ozone Layer Depletion, “Effects on Materials”

notes.front: A coastal fishing co-operative asks whether a small rise in UVB from ozone depletion could matter to them. What does the source say?
notes.back: Yes, it could: small increases could reduce populations of small marine organisms, with implications for the whole marine food chain.
notes.explanation: Note the hedge: the source says “could result in”, not “will”.
notes.evidence: Small increases in UVB exposure could result in population reductions for small marine organisms with implications for the whole marine food chain.
notes.source: US EPA, Health and Environmental Effects of Ozone Layer Depletion, “Effects on Marine Ecosystems”

notes.front: In the Antarctic, the amount of UVB measured at the surface can {{c1::double}} during the annual ozone hole.
notes.explanation: This is a measurement at the surface, where people, plants and animals are exposed, not high in the stratosphere.
notes.evidence: Studies have shown that in the Antarctic, the amount of UVB measured at the surface can double during the annual ozone hole.
notes.source: US EPA, Health and Environmental Effects of Ozone Layer Depletion, “The Connection between Ozone Layer Depletion and UVB Radiation”

notes.front: What is the Antarctic ozone “hole”, and since when has it appeared?
notes.back: Not a real hole but a large area of the stratosphere with extremely low ozone, seen each Antarctic spring since the early 1980s.
notes.explanation: The source gives it as one example of ozone depletion, and it recurs every year.
notes.evidence: over Antarctica that has occurred during the Antarctic spring since the early 1980s. This is not really a hole through the ozone layer, but rather a large area of the stratosphere with extremely low amounts of ozone.
notes.source: US EPA, Basic Ozone Layer Science, “II. Ozone Depletion”

notes.front: From when did scientific evidence show the ozone shield being depleted well beyond natural processes?
notes.back: From the 1970s.
notes.explanation: Before then, each natural reduction in ozone had been followed by a recovery; the depletion seen from the 1970s went beyond that.
notes.evidence: Each natural reduction in ozone levels has been followed by a recovery. Beginning in the 1970s, however, scientific evidence showed that the ozone shield was being depleted well beyond natural processes.
notes.source: US EPA, Basic Ozone Layer Science, “I. The Ozone Layer”

notes.front: Is ozone depletion limited to the area over the South Pole?
notes.back: No. It also occurs over the latitudes that include North America and Europe, among others.
notes.explanation: Research has found depletion over latitudes covering North America, Europe, Asia and much of Africa, Australia and South America.
notes.evidence: Ozone depletion is not limited to the area over the South Pole. Research has shown that ozone depletion occurs over the latitudes that include North America, Europe, Asia, and much of Africa, Australia, and South America.
notes.source: US EPA, Basic Ozone Layer Science, “II. Ozone Depletion”

notes.front: CFC versus HCFC: what differs in the molecule, and what does that mean for the ozone layer?
notes.back: An HCFC also contains hydrogen. Both contain chlorine and deplete ozone, but HCFCs to a much lesser extent.
notes.explanation: Chlorine is common to both, which is why both count as ozone-depleting; HCFCs were brought in as one class of replacement for CFCs.
notes.evidence: A compound consisting of hydrogen, chlorine, fluorine, and carbon. The HCFCs are one class of chemicals being used to replace the CFCs. They contain chlorine and thus deplete stratospheric ozone, but to a much lesser extent than CFCs.
notes.source: US EPA, Section 608 Technician Certification Test Topics, Core, “Environmental Impacts” (glossary entry “hydrochlorofluorocarbon”)

notes.front: HCFC versus HFC: which one depletes the ozone layer, and what makes the difference?
notes.back: The HCFC. An HFC contains no chlorine or bromine, so it does not deplete ozone and has an ODP of zero.
notes.explanation: Removing chlorine from the molecule removes the ozone-destroying atom; the other elements are shared.
notes.evidence: Because they do not contain chlorine or bromine, they do not deplete the ozone layer. All HFCs have an ozone depletion potential of 0.
notes.source: US EPA, Section 608 Technician Certification Test Topics, Core, “Environmental Impacts” (glossary entry “hydrofluorocarbon”)

notes.front: Class I versus class II substances: how do their phaseout schedules relate?
notes.back: Class II substances (the HCFCs) have a later phaseout schedule than class I.
notes.explanation: HCFCs were developed as transitional substitutes for class I ODS, and their schedule follows on from class I.
notes.evidence: HCFCs were developed as transitional substitutes for Class I ODS and are subject to a later phaseout schedule than Class I ODS.
notes.source: US EPA, Phaseout of Class II Ozone-Depleting Substances, introduction
